page.text:
A one-way implication $P \Rightarrow Q$ tells us that $P$ is a
*sufficient condition* for $Q$, and that $Q$ is a *necessary condition*
for $P$. Frequently in mathematics, however, two conditions are so
intimately linked that each implies the other. When both
$P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ hold, the statements $P$ and $Q$
stand or fall together.

This two-way implication is the *biconditional*, written
$P \Leftrightarrow Q$ and read *$P$ if and only if $Q$* (often
abbreviated as *$P$ iff $Q$*). The biconditional asserts that $P$ and $Q$
have identical truth values: both are true, or both are false. It is the
logical expression of *equivalence*. Most mathematical definitions are
implicit biconditionals: to say that a triangle is equilateral if and
only if all three of its sides have equal length is to establish a
complete mutual equivalence between the concept named and the condition
characterizing it.
